title: Images, Preimages, Cardinality, and Cantor
summary: Images (Bilder) and preimages (Urbilder) describe how functions transform subsets; injectivity (Injektivität) and surjectivity (Surjektivität) determine when equalities hold. We compare sets using injections, bijections, and the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem (Satz von Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder). The pairing function and diagonal argument show that some infinite sets are countable (abzählbar), while ℝ is uncountable (überabzählbar).
keyFacts: The image of a subset X ⊆ A is f(X) = {f(a) | a ∈ X}; the preimage of Y ⊆ B is f⁻¹(Y) = {a ∈ A | f(a) ∈ Y}.
The preimage operation is defined for every function and returns a set; it is not an inverse function.
Images preserve unions, and preimages preserve unions, intersections, and differences.
For every function, X ⊆ f⁻¹(f(X)) and f(f⁻¹(Y)) = Y ∩ im(f).
f is injective if and only if f⁻¹(f(X)) = X for every X ⊆ A.
f is surjective if and only if f(f⁻¹(Y)) = Y for every Y ⊆ B.
The relation a ≡f a′ if and only if f(a) = f(a′) is an equivalence relation; its class [a]f is f⁻¹({f(a)}).
|A| ≤ |B| means that an injection A → B exists; |A| = |B| means that a bijection exists.
By the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem, injections in both directions suffice to conclude |A| = |B|.
A set is countable if |A| ≤ |ℕ|; finite sets are included.
The Cantor pairing function assigns each pair in ℕ × ℕ a unique natural number; therefore, ℕ × ℕ is countable.
For every set A, |A| < |𝒫(A)|; the map a ↦ {a} is injective, but no map A → 𝒫(A) is surjective.
Cantor's diagonal set D = {a ∈ A | a ∉ g(a)} differs from every g(a) at least in whether it contains a.
Infinite bit sequences correspond to subsets of ℕ; Cantor's diagonal argument shows that they are uncountable.
ℕ, ℤ, and ℚ are countable, while ℝ is uncountable; finite and infinite bit sequences have different cardinalities.

review.notes: 44 Fragen geprüft. Beim Bild-Beispiel in „Anwenden“ war die Zielmenge B nicht angegeben; ergänzt B = {0,1,4,9}. Antworten, Distraktoren, Erklärungen und Prüfscripte stimmen.

questions.prompt: Given a function f: A → B and a subset X ⊆ A, what does f(X) denote?

options.text: The set of all values f(x) for x ∈ X
The set of all x ∈ A such that f(x) ∈ X
The unique function value of X
The set of all elements of B that have no preimage

questions.explanation: The image of X collects the function values of its elements. The set of elements with a particular output value is a preimage.

questions.prompt: For every function f: A → B, f⁻¹: B → A is an inverse function.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: An inverse function exists only for a bijection. By contrast, the preimage operation f⁻¹ on subsets of B is defined for every function.

questions.prompt: The image of the entire function f: A → B is denoted by ___.

options.text: A \\ f(A)
f⁻¹(B)
f(B)
im(f)

questions.explanation: The image is f(A), the set of values in B that are actually attained. It is also denoted by im(f).

questions.prompt: Let f: A → B be a function. Select all statements that always hold for arbitrary subsets.

options.text: f⁻¹(Y ∩ Y′) = f⁻¹(Y) ∩ f⁻¹(Y′)

questions.explanation: Images preserve unions; preimages preserve unions, intersections, and differences. In general, images preserve intersections only as an inclusion, not necessarily as an equality.

questions.prompt: Let f: A → B. Which statement about im(f) always holds?

options.text: im(f) = A
im(f) ⊆ B
im(f) = B
im(f) contains exactly one element

questions.explanation: All function values lie in the codomain B, so im(f) is a subset of B. It equals all of B exactly when f is surjective.

questions.prompt: For a total function f: A → B, f⁻¹(B) = A.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Every element of A is mapped to an element of B. Therefore, every element of A belongs to the preimage of the entire codomain.

questions.prompt: Which elements belong to the preimage of {r,b}?

context.caption: A function maps elements of A to elements of B.

options.text: {r,b}

questions.explanation: In the diagram, 1 and 5 map to r, and 3 maps to b. Elements 2 and 4 map to g, so they do not belong to the preimage.

questions.prompt: Which relation on A is induced by a function f: A → B when two elements are related exactly when they have the same function value?

options.text: a ≡f a′ if and only if a = f(a′)
a ≡f a′ if and only if a and a′ both belong to B
a ≡f a′ if and only if f(a) = f(a′)
a ≡f a′ if and only if f(a) ≠ f(a′)

questions.explanation: The function groups elements of its domain according to their function value. This relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

questions.prompt: |A| ≤ |B| holds if and only if there is an ___ from A to B.

options.text: inverse function
injection
surjection
equivalence relation

questions.explanation: An injection maps distinct elements of A to distinct elements of B. This shows that A has cardinality at most that of B.

questions.prompt: When is a set A called countable?

options.text: If A is a subset of ℝ
If there is a bijection A → ℕ and A is infinite
If |A| ≤ |ℕ|; finite sets are included
If every element of A can be computed algorithmically

questions.explanation: Countable means |A| ≤ |ℕ|, and thus includes both finite and countably infinite sets. Algorithmic computability is an additional property.

questions.prompt: Every proper subset of an infinite set has smaller cardinality than the entire set.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: For infinite sets, a proper subset can have the same cardinality: the positive even numbers are properly contained in ℕ, but n ↦ 2n is a bijection onto them.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$, $B=\{0,1,4,9\}$, and $f:A\to B$ be given by $f(x)=x^2$. Find the image of the subset $\{-2,1,2\}$. Function values that occur more than once are listed only once in the resulting set.
questions.explanation: The function values are $f(-2)=4$, $f(1)=1$, and $f(2)=4$. As a set, this gives $\{1,4\}$; the repeated value 4 is listed only once.

questions.prompt: Positive pairs $(n,m)$ are first ordered by increasing sum $n+m$. Along each diagonal, $n$ decreases while $m$ increases. Which pair comes immediately after $(1,3)$?

context.caption: Beginning of the diagonal enumeration of positive pairs

questions.explanation: The next diagonal has sum $n+m=5$. Its first pair has the largest possible $n$ and the smallest positive $m$: $(4,1)$.

questions.prompt: The Cantor pairing function is p(n,m) = m + ((n+m−1)(n+m−2))/2. Compute p(3,2).

source.heading: 6.1 Warum ist sogar $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ abzählbar?

questions.prompt: For z ∈ ℤ, let f(z) = 2z + 1 if z ≥ 0, and f(z) = −2z if z < 0. Compute f(−2).
questions.explanation: Since −2 < 0, f(−2) = −2 · (−2) = 4. In this way, negative integers are mapped to positive even numbers.

questions.prompt: Which rule defines a bijection from the positive natural numbers to the positive even numbers?

options.text: f(n) = n²
f(n) = 2n

questions.explanation: Each positive n maps to exactly one positive even number 2n, and each positive even number has exactly one preimage n = m/2.

questions.prompt: Select all statements that correctly describe comparisons of set sizes.

options.text: A bijection A → B shows |A| = |B|.
A single non-surjective injection A → B always shows |A| < |B|.
By CBS, two injections in opposite directions show |A| = |B|.
An injection A → B always shows |A| = |B|.
An injection A → B shows |A| ≤ |B|.

questions.explanation: Injections establish a cardinality inequality, while bijections establish equal cardinality. By Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder, injections in both directions suffice; a single non-surjective injection does not rule out a different bijection.

questions.prompt: f: A → B is surjective if and only if f(f⁻¹(Y)) = Y for every subset Y ⊆ B.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In general, f(f⁻¹(Y)) = Y ∩ im(f). This equals Y for every Y exactly when im(f) = B, that is, when f is surjective.

questions.prompt: For the equivalence relation induced by f, [a]f = ___.

options.text: im(f)

questions.explanation: The class of a contains exactly those elements of A that have the same function value as a. It is the preimage of the singleton set {f(a)}.

questions.prompt: Why can every rational number be represented uniquely as a reduced fraction z/m with z ∈ ℤ and m ∈ ℕ?

options.text: Because every rational number has exactly one integer denominator
Because the denominator is positive and the fraction is in lowest terms
Because all rational numbers have positive numerators
Because the set of rational numbers is finite

questions.explanation: With a positive denominator and a fraction in lowest terms, the representation is unique, including 0, which is represented as 0/1. This gives an injective map from ℚ into ℤ × ℕ.

questions.prompt: The set of all finite binary words is countably infinite.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: All finite binary words can be enumerated by a bijection with ℕ. This includes the empty word; infinite bit sequences, by contrast, are uncountable.

questions.prompt: The pairing function p enumerates pairs (n,m) ∈ ℕ × ℕ diagonally. Select all statements that explain why this correspondence is bijective.

options.text: The value of m determines the position within a diagonal.
Each diagonal n + m = s contains finitely many pairs.
The diagonals are assigned consecutive, disjoint blocks of numbers.
All pairs in one row are counted before the next row begins.

questions.explanation: Each diagonal is finite, the blocks cover the natural numbers without gaps, and m determines the position within a block. A whole infinite row is not traversed first.

questions.prompt: Why can f(X ∩ X′) be a proper subset of f(X) ∩ f(X′)?

options.text: Images always contain only one element.
The intersection of two sets is always empty.
A function does not have to preserve unions.
Different elements of X and X′ can have the same function value.

questions.explanation: A common image value can come from two different elements, one belonging only to X and the other only to X′. The value then belongs to the intersection of the images even though no common element was mapped.

questions.prompt: Let f: A → B. Select all statements that are each equivalent to f being injective.

options.text: f(A) = B.
For all X ⊆ A, f(A \\ X) = f(A) \\ f(X).
For all Y ⊆ B, f(f⁻¹(Y)) = Y.
For all X, X′ ⊆ A, f(X ∩ X′) = f(X) ∩ f(X′).
For all X ⊆ A, f⁻¹(f(X)) = X.

questions.explanation: Injectivity prevents distinct elements from having the same image, which makes the three statements about images hold. The condition involving all Y describes surjectivity.

questions.prompt: If there is a non-surjective injection A → B, it follows that |A| < |B|.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Such an injection shows only that |A| ≤ |B|. To establish a strict inequality, one must also rule out every bijection; a different bijection might exist.

questions.prompt: At what point in the proof is the assumed surjectivity of g: A → 𝒫(A) used?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  A[Assume g is surjective] --> B[Construct D from a with a not in g a]
  B --> C[D is a subset of A]
  C --> E[There is a d with g d equal to D]
  E --> F{Is d in D?}
  F --> G[By definition, d is not in D]
  F --> H[By definition, d is in D]
  G --> I[Contradiction]
  H --> I
context.caption: Proof steps for Cantor's diagonal argument.

options.text: When D ⊆ A implies D ∈ 𝒫(A)
When d ∈ D is used to conclude d ∉ D
When a d ∈ A with g(d) = D is assumed to exist
When D is defined as the set of elements a such that a ∉ g(a)

questions.explanation: Surjectivity means that every subset of A, in particular D, is attained as g(d) for some d ∈ A. This d then leads to the contradiction d ∈ D if and only if d ∉ D.

questions.prompt: Let g: A → 𝒫(A) and D = {a ∈ A | a ∉ g(a)}. What holds for every a ∈ A?

options.text: D and g(a) differ at least in whether they contain a.
D is not a subset of A.
D contains every element of g(a).
D = g(a) whenever a ∈ g(a).

questions.explanation: For every a, a ∈ D if and only if a ∉ g(a). Thus, D and g(a) differ at least in whether they contain a, so D cannot be a value of g.

source.heading: 7.3 Was genau ist an der Konstruktion so clever?

questions.prompt: Suppose a list assigns a bit sequence g(n) to each natural number n. Select all statements that correctly describe the diagonal counterexample.

options.text: The nth bit of the new sequence is flipped relative to the nth bit of g(n).
The new sequence differs from row n at least at position n.
Therefore, no such list can contain all infinite bit sequences.
The new sequence must agree with the first row.

questions.explanation: The negated diagonal differs from each row at that row's own diagonal position. Therefore, the list cannot be complete.

questions.prompt: Which two steps together prove the strict inequality |A| < |𝒫(A)| for every set A?

options.text: A surjection A → 𝒫(A) and the exclusion of every injection
An injection A → 𝒫(A) and the exclusion of every surjection A → 𝒫(A)
An injection 𝒫(A) → A and a bijection A → A
A bijection A → 𝒫(A)

questions.explanation: The embedding a ↦ {a} shows |A| ≤ |𝒫(A)|. The diagonal argument shows that no surjection A → 𝒫(A), and therefore no bijection, exists.

questions.prompt: Every real number has exactly one binary expansion, so the direct map from infinite bit sequences to [0,1] is injective.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Some numbers have two binary expansions, for example, 0,1000…₂ = 0,0111…₂. To establish equal cardinality, a careful construction is therefore needed, such as using injections in both directions and CBS.

questions.prompt: In the negated diagonal for a list of bit sequences, the nth bit is defined by dₙ = ___.

options.text: g(n)ₙ
1 − g(n)ₙ
g(n)ₙ − 1
1 + g(n)ₙ

questions.explanation: The bit is flipped: 0 becomes 1, and 1 becomes 0. Thus, the new sequence differs from the nth sequence at position n.

questions.prompt: What is the cardinality difference between {0,1}* and {0,1}^ℕ?

options.text: {0,1}* is countable, while {0,1}^ℕ is uncountable.
Both are countably infinite.
{0,1}* is uncountable, while {0,1}^ℕ is countable.
Both are finite.

questions.explanation: The asterisk denotes all finite binary words, which form a countable set. The exponent ℕ denotes infinite bit sequences; Cantor's diagonal argument shows that they are uncountable.

questions.prompt: Select all cardinality statements from the lecture unit that are true.
questions.explanation: The integers and rational numbers can be enumerated; the Cantor pairing function shows the same for ℕ × ℕ. By contrast, ℝ is uncountable.

questions.prompt: Let f: A → B and g: B → C be bijections. Which formula gives the inverse of their composition?

options.text: (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹
(g ∘ f)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹
(g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f ∘ g
(g ∘ f)⁻¹ = g ∘ f

questions.explanation: To undo the composition, apply g⁻¹ first and then f⁻¹. Therefore, the order of the composition is reversed.

questions.prompt: For a bijective function f, f⁻¹(f(X)) = X for every subset X ⊆ A.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Injectivity prevents additional elements from entering the preimage of the image. This property holds for all subsets exactly when f is injective; every bijection is injective.

questions.prompt: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $f:S\to S$ be given by $f(1)=2$, $f(2)=1$, $f(3)=4$, and $f(4)=3$. The directed function graph has the edge $x\to f(x)$ for each $x\in S$. Select all statements that hold for this map.

options.text: f is injective and therefore surjective.
f is surjective and therefore injective.
The directed function graph decomposes into disjoint cycles.
f is not a bijection.

questions.explanation: The function values are exactly the elements of $S$, each appearing once. Thus, $f$ is injective and surjective, hence bijective. The graph consists of the disjoint cycles $1\to2\to1$ and $3\to4\to3$; statement a is false.

questions.prompt: What conclusion follows from the depicted chain of cardinality comparisons?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  N["Natural numbers N"] -->|"Cantor: strictly smaller"| P["Power set of N"]
  P -->|"Characteristic functions"| B["Infinite bit sequences"]
  B -->|"Same cardinality"| I["Interval from 0 to 1"]
  I -->|"CBS and injections"| R["Real numbers R"]
context.caption: Comparing cardinalities up to the real numbers.

options.text: ℝ is uncountable because |ℕ| < |𝒫(ℕ)| = |ℝ|.
ℕ and ℝ have the same cardinality because both are infinite.
ℝ is countable because ℕ can be injected into 𝒫(ℕ).
𝒫(ℕ) is countable because it contains infinite bit sequences.

questions.explanation: Cantor's theorem gives |ℕ| < |𝒫(ℕ)|; characteristic functions identify 𝒫(ℕ) with infinite bit sequences, which have the same cardinality as ℝ. Thus, ℝ is uncountable.

questions.prompt: Select all steps that are part of the proof that ℚ is countable using reduced fractions.

options.text: This representation gives an injection ℚ → ℤ × ℕ.
Each rational number is encoded by its uniquely determined reduced fraction z/m with m > 0.
The density of ℚ in ℝ directly proves that ℚ is uncountable.
Since ℤ × ℕ is countable and ℕ injects into ℚ, CBS gives |ℚ| = |ℕ|.

questions.explanation: The unique reduced representation gives an injection into ℤ × ℕ. Since this product is countable and ℚ is infinite, the injection ℕ → ℚ and CBS yield equal cardinality.

questions.prompt: Let f: ℝ → (0,1) be given by f(x) = 1/(1 + 2⁻ˣ). Compute f(1).

questions.prompt: Suppose g: A → 𝒫(A) were surjective. With D = {a ∈ A | a ∉ g(a)} and g(d) = D, which statement leads to a contradiction?

options.text: d ∈ A if and only if d ∈ B
D = A for every function g
g(d) = {d} for every d ∈ A
d ∈ D if and only if d ∉ D

questions.explanation: By the definition of D, d ∈ D if and only if d ∉ g(d). Substituting g(d)=D gives d ∈ D if and only if d ∉ D, a contradiction to the assumed surjectivity.

questions.prompt: Since programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet, there are at most countably many programs. Because ℝ is uncountable, there exist real numbers that no program computes.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Finite strings over a finite alphabet are countable. Each program determines at most one real number, so not all real numbers can be computed.

questions.prompt: Select all correct pairings of the two distinct ideas associated with Cantor.

options.text: The diagonal argument flips diagonal bits in a purported complete list.
Both arguments show that all infinite sets have the same cardinality.
The pairing function enumerates pairs from ℕ × ℕ diagonally and shows that this set is countable.
The diagonal argument shows that no map A → 𝒫(A) is surjective.

questions.explanation: The pairing function assigns natural numbers to pairs without gaps. Cantor's diagonal argument, by contrast, constructs a subset that is not attained by any purported complete list of the power set.

questions.prompt: Given p(n,m) = m + ((n+m−1)(n+m−2))/2, the Cantor pairing function assigns a number to (n,m). What is p(1,3)?
questions.explanation: p(1,3) = 3 + ((3)(2))/2 = 6. The pair is in the third position on the diagonal n + m = 4, after the three pairs on the preceding diagonals.

questions.prompt: The fact that a set is countable guarantees that a program can enumerate its elements algorithmically.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Countability means that a bijection with a subset of ℕ exists. The enumeration need not be algorithmically computable; computability is an additional property.

levels.title: Practice: The Math Behind Everyday Life

questions.prompt: A transit app assigns each stop exactly one fare zone. You want to find all stops whose zone is A or C. Which search describes this?

options.text: All stops mapped to either zone A or C—the preimage of {A, C}.
Only the stops mapped to zone A.
All fare zones to which stops A or C are mapped.
An inverse function that assigns exactly one stop to each fare zone.

questions.explanation: You search the domain for all elements whose function value belongs to {A, C}: the preimage of this set of zones. The app does not need an inverse function; multiple stops can be assigned to the same zone.

questions.prompt: A contacts app converts each stored email address to lowercase and groups contacts when their converted addresses are the same. Which concept is involved?

options.text: Surjectivity: every conceivable email address must appear in the contact list.
A function-induced equivalence relation: contacts are grouped when they have the same function value.
An injective function: different contacts must receive different addresses.
An inverse function: each normalized address belongs to exactly one contact.

questions.explanation: Normalization is a function from contacts to addresses. “Maps to the same address” groups contacts into equivalence classes, which may contain multiple contacts.

questions.prompt: You have 8 independent smart home switches. Each is either on or off. How many different switch configurations are there?
questions.explanation: Each switch has 2 states. For 8 independent switches, there are $2^8=256$ configurations; each corresponds to a subset of the switches that are on.

questions.prompt: A ticketing system assigns each reserved seat a ticket ID from a specified set of valid IDs. What condition makes this assignment bijective?

options.text: Each seat receives its own ID, and each valid ID belongs to exactly one seat.
Every valid ID is used; multiple seats may share the same ID.
Each seat receives its own ID; some valid IDs may remain unused.
Each seat receives an ID; nothing is specified about duplicate or unused IDs.

questions.explanation: A bijection is both injective and surjective: there are no duplicate IDs, and every ID in the codomain is assigned. Condition b would give only injectivity, while condition c would give only surjectivity.

questions.prompt: In a database migration, two product catalogs A and B have different internal IDs. The team finds an injective map from A to B and also an injective map from B to A. The two maps are not inverses. What follows?

options.text: Nothing can be concluded about the sizes unless a direct bijection is given.
A and B have the same number of elements; a bijection exists by Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder.
A certainly has fewer elements than B because there is a map to B.
The catalogs have the same size only if the two maps are inverse functions of each other.

questions.explanation: By Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder, injections in opposite directions suffice to conclude that a bijection exists. The individual maps do not have to be inverse functions.

questions.prompt: A test network has 5 named devices. Each device is independently assigned to one of 3 Wi-Fi channels; multiple devices may use the same channel. How many assignments are possible?
questions.explanation: Each of the 5 devices has 3 independent choices. Thus, there are $3^5=243$ assignments, that is, functions from the set of devices to the set of channels.

questions.prompt: A test planner must eventually visit every pair of positive integer parameters $(i,j)$. A complete row with fixed $i$ is infinitely long. Which ordering still reaches every pair?

options.text: Visit all pairs with $i=1$ first, then those with $i=2$.
Traverse diagonals with constant $i+j$ one after another; each diagonal contains only finitely many pairs.
Visit only pairs with $i=j$.
Visit only pairs for which $i+j$ is prime.

questions.explanation: Enumerating by diagonals orders the pairs in $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ so that no infinite initial segment blocks the rest. The Cantor pairing function implements this idea as a unique numbering.

source.heading: 6.1 Warum ist sogar $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ abzählbar?

questions.prompt: A PIN consists of exactly four digits. Each position independently allows the digits 0 through 9; leading zeros and repetitions are allowed. How many different PINs are there?
questions.explanation: There are 10 possibilities for each of the four positions. The choices are independent, so there are $10\cdot10\cdot10\cdot10=10^4=10.000$ PINs.

questions.prompt: A service claims that the list $g(1),g(2),\ldots$ contains every infinite sequence of 0s and 1s. You form a new sequence by flipping the $n$th bit of $g(n)$ at position $n$. Why does this refute the claim?

options.text: The new sequence differs from each listed sequence at least at its own row number, so it is not on the list.
The new sequence is finite, whereas every listed sequence is infinite.
A list cannot contain repetitions, and flipping a bit creates repetitions.
Flipping a bit necessarily produces a sequence consisting only of ones.

questions.explanation: The diagonally constructed sequence differs from $g(n)$ at the $n$th bit. Therefore, it is missing from any purported complete list; this is Cantor's diagonal argument for the uncountability of infinite bit sequences.

questions.prompt: A fixed computational model treats each program as a finite text over a finite alphabet. Each program in this model specifies at most one real number. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: There are real numbers that no program in this model computes: programs are at most countable, whereas $\mathbb R$ is uncountable.
Every real number is computable because there are infinitely many possible programs.
There are more programs than real numbers because programs can be arbitrarily long.
The rational numbers are uncountable because fractions can have arbitrarily long numerators.

questions.explanation: All finite program texts can be enumerated, and each program here yields at most one number. Since the real numbers are uncountable, programs cannot describe every real number.
